3DROID: A Renderable 3D Gaussian Dataset with Measured Per-Scene Reliability

Wonguen Cho Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: wonguen.cho@snu.ac.kr    Junhoo Lee Affiliation: KAIST Email: nojunk@snu.ac.kr    Nojun Kwak Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: junhoo.lee@kaist.ac.kr
Abstract

Robot manipulation models primarily reason from 2D observations while acting in the 3D physical world. To bridge this gap, recent work has augmented robot data with geometric priors such as depth, point clouds, and 3D trajectories, while renderable 3D Gaussian representations provide another promising form of 3D supervision. However, 3DGS representation is designed mainly for photometric fidelity and may not preserve real-world metric scale, particularly when the supplied camera extrinsics are unreliable. We study the effect of extrinsic reliability and pose conditioning on feed-forward 3DGS, and propose a calibration-aware pipeline that anchors reconstructed scenes to the robot’s metric workspace. Our experiments show that pose conditioning improves novel-view fidelity, while its geometric benefit depends on the reliability of the injected extrinsics. Using this pipeline, we present a renderable, metric-pose-anchored dataset with scene-level reliability information for robot manipulation research. Our dataset is available at
https://huggingface.co/datasets/wonguen/3DROID

1 Introduction

Robot manipulation is inherently geometric: grasping and placement require reasoning about objects, free space, and motion in 3D. Explicit 3D representations improve spatial reasoning over 2D observations [10, 16, 17, 21], motivating recent 3D annotations and renderable robot scenes  [3, 13, 22]. Unlike point- or token-based annotations, renderable scenes provide a view-consistent appearance model from which observations and occlusions can be generated at new camera poses, enabling visual augmentation and simulation without additional data collection [22]. Such novel-view augmentation has also been shown to improve policy robustness to unseen camera poses [13].

Constructing these representations at dataset scale favors feed-forward reconstruction. Classical 3DGS optimizes each scene independently from its available observations, making sparse robot views underconstrained and requiring repeated optimization over thousands of episodes  [8]. Feed-forward variants instead amortize reconstruction across training scenes: their learned priors support inference from limited views, while a single forward pass avoids repeated per-scene optimization  [7, 11, 18, 19]. This makes them a practical basis for constructing large-scale renderable robot datasets.

These advantages address sparsity and computational cost, but not physical reliability. Both classical and feed-forward 3DGS are developed primarily for photorealistic novel-view synthesis. For manipulation, however, synthesized observations are useful only if they remain consistent with the metric workspace in which robot states and actions are defined [17]. A reconstruction may preserve appearance while silently moving surfaces or changing scene scale. Moreover, camera calibrations in real-world robot datasets are not uniformly reliable, so shipped poses cannot simply be treated as ground truth. Whether the resulting scenes preserve metric scale therefore remains unclear, and calibration must be validated independently of the reconstructor.

Prior work addresses parts of this problem from complementary directions. Geometry-aware Gaussian methods introduce surface constraints, stereo cues, or 3D priors to improve geometric stability [5, 14, 13], while camera-refinement methods align visual observations with robot geometry [6]. Yet these model- and calibration-level solutions do not by themselves specify how reliability should be communicated when reconstructions are released as data. This leaves a dataset-level question: how can calibration suitability and reconstruction reliability be measured and exposed for each scene?

In this paper, we therefore build 3DROID by reconstructing DROID [9] with pose-conditioned feed-forward 3DGS and separating photometric fidelity from physical consistency. Building on robot–depth alignment used for camera refinement [6], we validate calibration before reconstruction and separately assess geometric reliability afterward, together with measurement coverage. This separates calibration suitability from reconstruction reliability. We therefore release measured support rather than claim geometric ground truth or downstream policy gains. Table 1 summarizes the scene-level assets added by 3DROID and the source modalities that remain in DROID.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We release 3DROID, a DROID-derived dataset of renderable 3D Gaussian scenes with per-scene calibration and reconstruction-reliability metadata.

  • •

    We empirically show that metric pose conditioning anchors reconstruction scale to the physical workspace and yields median per-scene PSNR gains of +0.73+0.73 to +2.73+2.73 dB at a fixed extrinsic source.

  • •

    We repurpose robot–depth consistency as a coverage-aware reconstruction evaluation protocol that compares rendered 3DGS depth with classical stereo and kinematically localized robot geometry.

2 Related works

3D representations for robotics.

Explicit 3D observations improve spatial reasoning for manipulation. DP3 demonstrated this with sparse point cloud, and FP3 scaled point-cloud pretraining to DROID [16, 20]. DROID-3D added depth and point clouds, while 4D-VLA and Lift3D-VLA incorporated temporal geometry [3, 10, 21]. PointWorld and Robo3R further improved calibration and robot-frame alignment [6, 17]. Yet these point- or token-based outputs lack a view-consistent appearance model. Unlike point observations, renderable scenes can synthesize view-consistent observations from new camera poses, expose viewpoint-dependent visibility, and support data augmentation or visual simulation without recollecting demonstration. RoboSnap builds layered mesh–Gaussian scenes from a single image, but does not provide measured per-scene reconstruction reliability [22]. This leaves open how to construct renderable robot scenes while explicitly measuring their metric alignment and reconstruction reliability.

Feedforward Gaussian Splatting.

Whereas per-scene 3DGS requires time-consuming optimization [8], feed-forward methods leverage learned priors to reconstruct scenes from sparse views in a single pass [1, 7]. Regardless of reconstruction strategy, 3DGS is designed primarily for photorealistic novel-view rendering. Yet photorealism and manipulation readiness are different objectives: novel-view fidelity does not guarantee metric scale, robot-frame alignment, or reliable geometry. Pose-conditioned PixelSplat, MVSplat, and DepthSplat improve matching and depth estimation but assume reliable calibration [1, 2, 15]. NoPoSplat and AnySplat remove pose inputs, while YoNoSplat handles variable posed or unposed inputs and ZipSplat compresses the representation [7, 11, 18, 19]. GenSplat applies this pose-free paradigm to robotic view augmentation, but evaluates DROID reconstruction only qualitatively without testing robot-frame alignment [13]. We instead audit calibration and evaluate rendering separately from stereo-supported geometry.

3 Robot-Anchored 3D Reconstruction

3.1 Pose-Free Feed-Forward Gaussian Reconstruction

Feed-forward Gaussian reconstructors predict a 3D Gaussian scene from a set of source-view inputs. For scene ee, let 𝒳e\mathcal{X}_{e} denote the native pose-free input of a backbone. The reconstructor predicts

𝒢^e=Fθ​(𝒳e),I^e​t=ℛ⁡(𝒢^e,ξe​t),\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{e}=F_{\theta}(\mathcal{X}_{e}),\qquad\widehat{I}_{et}=\mathcal{R}\!\left(\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{e},\xi_{et}\right), (1)

where ξe​t\xi_{et} denotes a target camera configuration and I^e​t\widehat{I}_{et} is the corresponding rendered image. These models are trained to minimize target-view image discrepancy,

θ⋆=arg⁡minθ​𝔼e,t​[dimg​(I^e​t,Ie​t)],\theta^{\star}=\arg\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{e,t}\left[d_{\mathrm{img}}\left(\widehat{I}_{et},I_{et}\right)\right], (2)

where dimgd_{\mathrm{img}} denotes the model-specific image-space training objective. Thus, pose-free feed-forward reconstruction learns a scene whose renderings agree with images from held-out viewpoints.

3.2 3D Reconstruction from a Robot Manipulation Perspective

Image-space supervision does not by itself provide a global metric reference. Let

𝐒⁡(𝐱)=s​𝐑𝐱+𝐭,𝐒∈Sim⁡(3),s>0,𝐑∈SO⁡(3).\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{x})=s\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{t},\qquad\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{Sim}(3),\quad s>0,\quad\mathbf{R}\in\mathrm{SO}(3). (3)

Applying the same global similarity transform to a scene and its camera configuration preserves the rendered images:

ℛ⁡(𝒢^e,𝒞e)=ℛ⁡(𝐒⋅𝒢^e,𝐒⋅𝒞e).\mathcal{R}(\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{e},\mathcal{C}_{e})=\mathcal{R}\!\left(\mathbf{S}\!\cdot\!\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{e},\mathbf{S}\!\cdot\!\mathcal{C}_{e}\right). (4)

Consequently, image-only reconstruction is determined only up to a global Sim⁡(3)\mathrm{Sim}(3) transformation.

Robot manipulation instead requires a metric reconstruction anchored to the robot base frame 𝖡\mathsf{B}. Let 𝐏e​i𝖡\mathbf{P}_{ei}^{\mathsf{B}} be a robot-surface point obtained by applying forward kinematics to joint state 𝐪e\mathbf{q}_{e} and CAD point 𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i},

𝐏e​i𝖡=FK⁡(𝐪e;𝐜i).\mathbf{P}_{ei}^{\mathsf{B}}=\operatorname{FK}(\mathbf{q}_{e};\mathbf{c}_{i}). (5)

For the ideal base-to-camera extrinsic (𝐑e​v⋆,𝐭e​v⋆)(\mathbf{R}^{\star}_{ev},\mathbf{t}^{\star}_{ev}), this physical point projects to

𝐱e​i​v⋆\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{eiv} =𝐑e​v⋆​𝐏e​i𝖡+𝐭e​v⋆,\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}^{\star}_{ev}\mathbf{P}_{ei}^{\mathsf{B}}+\mathbf{t}^{\star}_{ev}, (6)

De​vtrue​(𝐮e​i​v⋆)\displaystyle D^{\mathrm{true}}_{ev}\left(\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{eiv}\right) =ze​i​v⋆.\displaystyle=z^{\star}_{eiv}.

This condition defines the desired metric anchor: robot geometry expressed in 𝖡\mathsf{B} must agree with the corresponding camera-depth observation.

3.3 Dataset Curation via Calibration Consistency Validation

However, DROID camera poses can be noisy [6], so even a refined pose cannot be assumed to be a reliable metric reference. We therefore replace the unavailable ideal quantities in Eq. 6 with classical stereo depth and validate each candidate pose source pp at projected robot points. For each valid robot-point projection, we compute

𝐱e​i​vp\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{p}_{eiv} =𝐑e​vp​𝐏e​i𝖡+𝐭e​vp,\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}^{p}_{ev}\mathbf{P}_{ei}^{\mathsf{B}}+\mathbf{t}^{p}_{ev}, (7)
𝐮e​i​vp\displaystyle\mathbf{u}^{p}_{eiv} =π(𝐊e​v𝐱pe​i​v),zpe​i​v=[𝐱pe​i​v]z,\displaystyle=\pi\!\left(\mathbf{K}_{ev}\mathbf{x}^{p}_{eiv}\right),\qquad z^{p}_{eiv}=[\mathbf{x}^{p}_{eiv}]_{z},
re​i​vp\displaystyle r^{p}_{eiv} =De​vst​(𝐮e​i​vp)ze​i​vp.\displaystyle=\frac{D^{\mathrm{st}}_{ev}\left(\mathbf{u}^{p}_{eiv}\right)}{z^{p}_{eiv}}.

Here De​vstD^{\mathrm{st}}_{ev} is the stereo depth map and 𝒜ep\mathcal{A}_{e}^{p} contains projections that are in crop and have valid stereo depth. We aggregate the partial observations using the robust scene-level statistic

ρep=median(i,v)∈𝒜ep⁡re​i​vp,\rho_{e}^{p}=\operatorname{median}_{(i,v)\in\mathcal{A}_{e}^{p}}r^{p}_{eiv}, (8)

and retain the scenes satisfying

ℰvalidp={e||𝒜ep|≥nmin,τmin≤ρep≤τmax}.\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{valid}}^{p}=\left\{e\;\middle|\;|\mathcal{A}_{e}^{p}|\geq n_{\min},\quad\tau_{\min}\leq\rho_{e}^{p}\leq\tau_{\max}\right\}. (9)

For a pose-compatible reconstructor, the validated camera configuration is then used for pose-conditioned reconstruction,

𝒢^e𝖡=Fθ​(𝒳e,𝒞ep),e∈ℰvalidp,\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{\mathsf{B}}_{e}=F_{\theta}\!\left(\mathcal{X}_{e},\mathcal{C}_{e}^{p}\right),\qquad e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{valid}}^{p}, (10)

where 𝒞ep={𝐊e​v,[𝐑e​vp∣𝐭e​vp]}v∈𝒱e\mathcal{C}_{e}^{p}=\{\mathbf{K}_{ev},[\mathbf{R}^{p}_{ev}\mid\mathbf{t}^{p}_{ev}]\}_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{e}}.

4 3DROID

4.1 Configuration

DROID is widely used in recent manipulation research [9]. We group its roughly 35k successful episodes by (lab,serial1,serial2,date)(\mathrm{lab},\mathrm{serial}_{1},\mathrm{serial}_{2},\mathrm{date}) and sample one episode per group, yielding 520 scene groups. From these scenes, 225 scenes contain the four stereo videos and trajectory record required by our gate. Applying the calibration gate in Eq. 9 with nmin=30n_{\min}=30 valid projections and (τmin,τmax)=(0.85,1.15)(\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max})=(0.85,1.15) retains 114 scenes under the refined pose source and 80 under the shipped one. We release the former.

As summarized in Table 1, 3DROID augments each retained episode with a pose-conditioned ZipSplat reconstruction [11], rendered depth and coverage maps, camera parameters, and per-scene reliability measurements. We perform no new camera calibration: intrinsics and shipped extrinsics come from DROID, while PointWorld provides the refined left-eye extrinsics [6], and corresponding right-eye poses are derived using the original stereo transform. All parameters are packaged in a common camera-to-world convention, and source videos and robot states remain accessible through the DROID episode key.

Four released scenes contain all-zero DROID intrinsics and yield no valid evaluation measurements, leaving 110 scenes for photometric evaluation. One additional scene uses per-serial median intrinsics from 501 other DROID episodes and is retained. All five cases are explicitly flagged. Geometric comparisons involving shipped extrinsics use 109 scenes because one further scene lacks valid robot support, whereas comparisons within refined extrinsics use 110.

4.2 Evaluation

Baselines

We evaluate ZipSplat [11] and YoNoSplat [18] at their native resolutions. Baseline is pose-free with DROID extrinsics, whereas Ours is pose-conditioned with refined rig extrinsics. We report geometric results for both backbones to assess whether the same trend holds across models. In pose-free runs, the backbone reconstructs the scene from RGB alone and predicts its own camera frame. The selected extrinsics are applied only after reconstruction to register this predicted frame and place the held-out camera for evaluation. They are not network inputs.

Settings

Photometric evaluation reconstructs from ext1L, ext1R, and ext2L, and reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on held-out ext2R. Because the feed-forward backbones use the first input view as their frame coordinate, we place ext1L first and hold out ext2R, which has the largest viewpoint separation from this anchor and thus provides a more discriminative evaluation [7, 12]. Geometric evaluation separately reconstructs from all four exterior views and reports robot-surface depth error and dense disagreement with classical stereo [4], both with coverage. The wrist stream is excluded from both evaluations. Dense stereo applies consistency and low-texture filtering and is treated as input-view agreement, not ground truth. All reported p-values are from two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on paired per-scene differences, with the scene as the unit of variability.

4.2.1 Quantitative Results

Photometric Fidelity.

Table 2 compares our pose-conditioned, refined-extrinsic configuration with the default pose-free baseline on held-out ext2R. Across 110 scenes, PSNR increases from 12.5712.57 to 15.8115.81 (+3.24+3.24 dB) for YoNoSplat and from 12.7512.75 to 16.2716.27 (+3.52+3.52 dB) for ZipSplat. SSIM also increases and LPIPS decreases for both backbones. This consistent trend shows that the photometric gain is not specific to the ZipSplat release backbone. Because this end-to-end comparison changes both the extrinsic source and pose conditioning, Table 4 separates their individual effects.

Geometric Fidelity.

Table 3 reports two complementary measures of geometric consistency. Robot Projection Coverage reports the fraction of these queries that fall inside the evaluation image and pass the rendered-alpha threshold. It measures evaluation support rather than reconstruction completeness or accuracy. Robot Error compares the 3DGS-rendered depth at kinematically projected robot-surface queries with the camera-axis depth predicted by forward kinematics and CAD. Stereo Disagreement compares rendered depth with confidence-filtered SGBM depth over their jointly valid pixels.

Pose conditioning alone does not consistently improve these measurements. With shipped DROID extrinsics, pose conditioning slightly lowers both YoNoSplat errors. For ZipSplat, the aggregate robot-error median rises from 19.7119.71 to 30.5830.58 cm while stereo disagreement decreases. However, the paired robot-error change is not significant (median Δ=−1.10\Delta=-1.10 cm, p=0.072p=0.072, n=109n=109). Thus, the aggregate increase does not establish systematic degradation but reflects heterogeneous scene-level responses. With refined extrinsics, aggregate errors decrease for ZipSplat and remain nearly unchanged for YoNoSplat. Robot projection coverage is identical between pose-free and pose-conditioned reconstruction within each extrinsic source, so these differences are measured over the same projected support.

4.2.2 Qualitative Results

Qualitative Results.

Figure 2 compares the pose-free DROID baseline with Ours, which combines refined extrinsics and pose conditioning. All scenes are reconstructed from three exterior views and rendered at the held-out ext2R camera. Across the examples, the baseline often exhibits viewpoint misalignment and scene distortion, whereas Ours more closely matches the ground-truth viewing direction and produces fewer visible artifacts. Because both the extrinsic source and pose conditioning change in this comparison, the figure demonstrates their combined effect rather than attributing the improvement to either component.

4.2.3 Ablation Studies

Quantitative Ablation.

Table 4 separates the effects of pose conditioning and refined extrinsics using paired per-scene differences. At a fixed extrinsic source, pose conditioning improves all three photometric metrics for both supported backbones, with median per-scene PSNR gains ranging from +0.73+0.73 to +2.73+2.73 dB (all PSNR p<10−10p<10^{-10}). At a fixed pose setting, switching to refined extrinsics yields median PSNR gains of +0.29+0.29 to +2.13+2.13 dB and likewise improves SSIM and LPIPS (all p<2×10−8p<2\times 10^{-8}). Combining both components performs best for YoNoSplat and ZipSplat, although their gains are non-additive.

Of the 110 valid-intrinsic scenes, AnySplat is evaluated on 107 because its pose-free camera estimator produces degenerate camera layouts in three cases, preventing reliable alignment to the metric camera rig. AnySplat gains +0.39+0.39 dB under the same shipped-to-refined contrast. This change reflects scene registration and held-out camera placement rather than pose conditioning.

Qualitative Ablation.

As shown in Figure 3, the two DROID-calibrated results exhibit scene distortion and viewpoint misalignment relative to the ground truth, whereas the refined-extrinsic results recover a more consistent viewing angle. For ZipSplat, the four settings achieve PSNR values of 9.819.81, 10.8510.85, 14.8614.86, and 14.9714.97 dB, respectively. Despite the similar scores of the last two settings, the pose-free result exposes more of the washing machine’s left panel, while Ours more closely matches the ground-truth framing. YoNoSplat shows the same overall tendency, with PSNR increasing from 8.498.49 dB at Baseline to 15.7315.73 dB with Ours. This comparison supports the quantitative ablation while revealing local viewpoint errors that PSNR alone may obscure.

Gate-Threshold Sensitivity.

Table 5 shows that 114 is determined by the selected operating point rather than being an intrinsic dataset size. The pass count nearly saturates beyond a ±20%\pm 20\% ratio band, whereas changing the minimum support has a larger effect, indicating that scene selection is governed primarily by robot observability. Refined extrinsics yield more passing scenes than shipped extrinsics under every tested setting, although this ordering measures gate consistency rather than independent absolute pose accuracy.

4.2.4 Robustness Checks

The calibration gain extends beyond the probe comparing robot geometry with depth. Although PointWorld does not optimize rendering fidelity [6], refined extrinsics yield median paired PSNR gains of +2.13+2.13, +1.42+1.42, and +0.39+0.39 dB for ZipSplat, YoNoSplat, and AnySplat (n=110,110,107n=110,110,107), with SSIM and LPIPS agreeing. Because AnySplat does not consume poses, its fixed Gaussians isolate improvements in registration between the camera and the scene. A secondary ext1L test split by the median maximum left-camera correction (11.2311.23 cm; n=109n=109) yields +0.89+0.89 dB for the larger-correction half and +0.00+0.00 dB for the smaller half.

Photometry still does not establish metric placement. Under shipped extrinsics without pose conditioning, robot-depth ratios are 1.341.34, 1.311.31, and 1.261.26 for the same backbones, consistently placing the arm too far. This motivates our robot-referenced metric and per-scene reliability annotations.

5 Discussion and Limitations

3DROID currently reconstructs a single static frame from four exterior views and measures geometry only where robot-surface or stereo support is available. Additional well-calibrated views may reduce sparse-view ambiguity, but we do not isolate this effect. We exclude the wrist stream because its narrow field of view and large domain gap from stationary cameras are poorly matched to current feed-forward backbones. Adapting these models to mixed observations from exterior and wrist cameras, or fine-tuning them on robot data with metric pose, stereo, kinematic, and CAD supervision, is promising future work. A natural extension is to expand 3DROID from static snapshots to temporally consistent 4D scenes that could provide dynamic context to robot learning models. We do not claim full-scene geometric ground truth or downstream manipulation improvements.

6 Conclusion

To complement 2D-centric robot manipulation data with explicit 3D scene information, we studied how to construct 3D Gaussian representations anchored to the metric scale and coordinate frame of real-world workspaces. Our experiments show that pose conditioning constrains global similarity ambiguity, while its outcome depends critically on the reliability of the injected extrinsics and does not alone guarantee metric geometry. We therefore assess physical consistency separately through coverage-aware agreement between rendered depth, classical stereo, and kinematically localized robot geometry. Based on these findings, we introduce 3DROID, a metric-pose-anchored dataset that provides renderable robot scenes together with measured calibration and reconstruction-reliability information.

Appendix A Additional experimental details

A.1 Compute resources and runtime

All experiments used a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU. Model loading took 20.7 s, and the first scene required approximately 250 s for one-time CUDA kernel compilation. Excluding these initialization costs, reconstruction took a median of 0.77 s per scene across all 114 released scenes. The reported compute also includes preliminary and repeated experiments conducted during model selection, ablation, and debugging.

A.2 Released Code and Reproducibility

The released dataset provides the 114 episode identifiers, a pinned software environment, the unmodified ZipSplat source, checkpoint revision and checksum, and a resumable pipeline for rebuilding the released four-view Gaussians and depth maps from externally obtained DROID videos and camera metadata. It also reconstructs the three-view held-out ext2R renderings under the four pose–extrinsic conditions. Running python pipeline/run_pipeline.py all performs frame extraction, reconstruction, rendering, and verification. On our reference A100 environment, all 114 scenes reproduce the stored depth, alpha, camera, and metric-scale arrays exactly. PLY hashes are reported separately because atomic rasterization need not be byte-identical across hardware.

For verification without raw videos or a GPU, python evaluation/make_tables.py --bundle . re-aggregates the released per-scene measurements and reproduces the ZipSplat entries in Tables 2, 3, and 4, including their sample counts. This operation verifies the reported aggregation rather than re-measuring geometry. The current release does not rerun the YoNoSplat and AnySplat baselines. The required external inputs are documented in the release README.

Appendix B Asset Licenses and Data Availability

Existing assets.

We use publicly released datasets and pretrained reconstruction models under their respective terms. DROID [9], including the source images, robot states, intrinsics, and shipped extrinsics, is released under CC BY 4.0. We redistribute only the camera parameters required to use 3DROID; the source images and robot states remain in DROID and are joined through the episode UUID. We use the droid_raw v1.0.1 release, accessed at gs://gresearch/robotics/droid_raw/1.0.1/.

The refined left-eye extrinsics are obtained from PointWorld-DROID [6] under the NVIDIA License. We use the PointWorld-DROID release at revision dd9aaeec94bb14e27ab6b16b6e4aa0dbcf3ef56f. The corresponding right-eye poses are derived using the original within-rig stereo transform. In accordance with Sections 3.1–3.3 of that license, we include the complete license, preserve upstream attribution, identify the derived assets, and retain its restriction to non-commercial research or evaluation.

Reconstruction models.

The released reconstructions use the official ZipSplat checkpoint zipsplat-da3g-252p.tar [11]. ZipSplat code is licensed under Apache-2.0 and its pretrained weights under CC BY-NC 4.0. YoNoSplat [18] and AnySplat [7] are used only as experimental baselines; their official code is licensed under MIT. Model code and pretrained weights are obtained from the original repositories and are not redistributed in 3DROID.

3DROID release.

The 114-scene 3DROID dataset is publicly available during review at https://huggingface.co/datasets/wonguen/3DROID. Documentation and author-provided release material are licensed under Apache-2.0. To the extent that we hold the relevant rights, the generated Gaussian, depth, and measurement assets are released under CC BY-NC 4.0, while remaining subject to applicable upstream terms. Camera metadata retains its component-specific DROID and PointWorld terms. The repository includes the corresponding license files and third-party notices and will be de-anonymized in the camera-ready release.

The repository additionally includes the reconstruction and verification scripts, pinned dependencies, episode list, per-file manifest, and numerical reproduction records.

The release vendors only the unmodified ZipSplat source under Apache-2.0. YoNoSplat and AnySplat code and checkpoints are not included; their official repositories, revisions, and checkpoint hashes are provided for provenance.
